The night was thin over Paris, a sheet of darkness that pressed against the iron lattice of the Eiffel Tower as if it were trying to climb into the heart of the city itself. Pierre stood on the unfinished upper platform, his boots gripping the cold rail like a lifeline. The wind slipped through the gaps between girders with a hiss that sounded almost like a warning.

He could hear the distant clang of rivets below and the low rumble of steam engines that powered the hand‑driven hammers used to drive iron together. Every vibration seemed to travel up his spine, reminding him that he was standing on metal that had been lifted by machines that could not lift a man as easily.

It was only a few hours before the Exposition Universelle opened its doors to the world, and Pierre knew he had to finish his rivets before dawn. The last section of the upper platform still needed a series of fasteners to lock two large iron girders together. Leclerc, the foreman who watched him from below like a hawk, had given him no instructions beyond “Finish it by sunrise.” No mention of any modifications or extra work.

Pierre’s fear of heights had been a secret he carried for months. He’d climbed ladders and swung on rope harnesses every day since the construction began, but he never let Leclerc see the tremor in his hands or the way his eyes would dart to the edge whenever the wind blew too hard. “You’re fine,” Leclerc had said when Pierre first started. “No need for that.”

Now the fear clawed at him again as if it had been a part of him all along. He pressed his palms to the rail, feeling the metal’s cold under his skin. The wind was a whisper against his ears, and he could almost hear it saying, *“Do you have what it takes?”* It wasn’t just the height that terrified him; it was the idea that if he slipped, the world below would crush him.

The joint Pierre had to work on was not in any of the plans he’d studied. The engineers’ calculations had left a small gap where the angle between two beams seemed slightly off. He believed the stress there would be greater than anticipated. In his mind, adding an extra rivet could prevent the tower from sagging later, but Leclerc’s orders were clear: no changes.

He slipped a single hammer and a spare rivet out of his apron—something no one else would have seen if they weren’t looking at the other end of the platform—and set the rivet between the two beams. The metal rang once, a thin bell that cut through the night’s hush. He tapped it carefully with the hammer until the metal was sealed in place, the extra fastener hidden beneath the workman's coat.

He worked through the night, each rivet a tiny battle against his fear and the pressure to finish on time. Between taps he clutched the rail as if it were a lifeline, looking out over Paris below where lanterns flickered like distant stars. The air smelled of oil and iron, and the cold stone of the tower pressed up into him.

At 2 a.m., Leclerc appeared at the edge of the platform, his silhouette sharp against the moonlit sky. He inspected the work with a quick glance; no one else had seen Pierre’s secret addition. “Good,” he said, voice low but firm. “Finish it before sunrise.” Pierre nodded, breath shallow.

“Keep your hands steady,” Leclerc warned, as if to remind him of the danger. He turned away, leaving Pierre alone with his thoughts and his fear. The foreman’s words rang in Pierre’s ears like a warning from the past: he had hidden this secret for months because he feared being seen as weak.

Pierre returned to his work. Each rivet was hammered into place with a rhythm that felt almost like breathing. The platform above him seemed to pulse under his feet, as if it were alive and listening. He could feel the tremor of the tower itself in his bones.

The first light of dawn crept across the iron lattice like a pale finger. Paris woke with a muted hum; people began to spill into streets below. Pierre’s heart hammered harder than ever. He could see, for the first time since he had hidden his fear, how small and fragile the world looked from up there. The wind that had once seemed so fierce now sounded like a distant memory.

He finished the last rivet with shaking hands. He felt the weight of relief as the metal snapped into place. Then he leaned back against the rail, breathing slowly, feeling the cool air on his face. For a moment, he let himself feel the fear that had always been there, and then let it go.

When the tower opened to the public at 6 a.m., Leclerc came early, as was his habit. He walked up the iron stairway with the same caution he’d used that night, but this time he stopped before the unfinished upper platform. He looked down at the joint where Pierre had added an extra rivet.

The sight made him pause. The rivet was not in any plan; it was a small, neat addition that had been hidden by Pierre’s careful work. Leclerc’s face went pale, then tightened with a mix of surprise and unease. He stared at the metal until he could no longer deny what he saw: the tower, which had always seemed to defy gravity, now bore an extra layer of strength.

“Pierre?” he called out softly. The word carried across the wind.

No answer came. Pierre was already gone from his post, having vanished into the night. Leclerc stood there for a long time, staring at the rivet as if it were a secret held by a ghost. Then, with a heavy sigh, he turned and walked back down to the ground, knowing that whatever had happened on that platform would not be forgotten.

**The Last Rivet**

March 28, 1889

The Seine shivered under a pale morning sky as workers gathered at the Champ de Mars, their bodies moving like a living machine of iron and sweat. Far above them, the Eiffel Tower—still an unfinished lattice of steel—reached toward the clouds, its beams glinting in the early light.

Pierre Dubois stood on a scaffold, his gloves stained black from years of shaping metal. He had left Brittany for Paris two years earlier, carrying with him only a promise etched on his father's calloused hand: “If you build the iron, you will earn honor.” Now he was earning it, one rivet at a time.

He worked ten hours a day for 1½ francs—a modest wage that kept their cramped apartment in Rue de l'Ancienne Légion just on time. The tower’s construction had already taken two years and nine months, from March 28, 1887 to this very day, under the guidance of Gustave Eiffel’s company. By now, about 300 men and women—blacksmiths, riveters, ironworkers—had poured their sweat into its frame.

The fourth tier of beams had just been hoisted into place, but the final row of rivets that would lock it solidly still waited on a line of iron plates. Each rivet was a small, flat disk about an inch across, waiting to be hammered between two pieces of wrought iron. The entire structure relied on 18 038 of these tiny metal soldiers.

Jean‑Baptiste, the foreman with a scar above his left eyebrow, called out over the clangs of metal. “Listen up! The World’s Fair opens on March 31—three days left. Every rivet counts.”

A hush fell. Pierre felt the weight of his own ribs press against his chest as if someone were standing behind him.

He had always imagined finishing a structure would be an act of triumph, but here it was a race against time, wind, and iron. His wife, Marie, waited for him at their small apartment on Rue de l'Ancienne Légion. She was pregnant, her belly swollen like a small moon. Her mother had warned them that any delay would mean she might have to wait until after birth to move back into their home. Pierre could not bear the thought of her waiting longer than necessary.

“Je ferai tout ce qu’il faut,” he whispered as he tightened his leather gloves, feeling the roughness of iron on his fingers. “I will finish this.”

He looked at the rivets that lay out like a row of tiny soldiers awaiting orders. Each one was a promise: safety, progress, and his own future.

Jean‑Baptiste approached him, clapping him on the back. “Good! Now get to work.” He added, with a grin that betrayed his pride in the men under his command, “You’ll earn an extra five francs for finishing early.”

Pierre nodded, feeling a surge of determination. The tower would be finished before the World’s Fair opened—a promise he was determined to keep.

He climbed up the scaffold, each step creaking under his weight. The wind had already begun to pick up, whispering through the gaps between beams like a secret. He could feel the temperature drop as he rose higher.

At this height, the air was thinner, the ground far below. He could see the Seine’s waves moving like a living thing and the city of Paris stretching out beneath him—church spires, cobblestone streets, gas lamps beginning to glow in the distance. The tower itself seemed to stand on its own, an iron spine against the sky.

He reached for his hammer—a heavy wooden mallet that had been passed down through generations. He could hear the clang of metal hitting metal, a rhythm he had grown accustomed to. It was almost hypnotic. But each strike was a reminder: the tower’s final shape rested on this moment.

Pierre positioned himself beside the beam, aligning it with precision. The rivet lay between the iron plates, waiting to be hammered into place. He lifted his arm, feeling the strain in his shoulders. The first hammer blow rang out. He followed up with the second. The metal clanged and bent slightly; the rivet slipped a little.

He was halfway through when he heard the sound of a fellow worker’s scream from below. He looked down. A man named Jules had lost his footing on the scaffold rail, the rope harness that held him to the iron framework failing for a moment before catching again. Jules’ body hung in midair for a moment before he hit the iron frame with a sickening thud.

The others froze, then resumed their work with renewed caution. The incident served as a stark reminder that they were not just building a structure; they were risking their lives for it. Safety nets had been installed along the lower levels, but the high scaffolding still held little in its grasp. A rope net hung like a spiderweb beneath them, and each worker’s harness was a thin lifeline.

Pierre felt his heart hammering against his chest. He remembered his father telling him: “You are strong, Pierre, but you must be careful.” The memory steadied him. He took another rivet and hammered it with more force, feeling the metal’s heat on his palm.

The day slipped away into night. The tower gleamed under gas lamps that painted a golden halo around its iron ribs. Workers who had been exhausted during the day now moved with new urgency, their faces illuminated by lanterns as they worked in the dim glow.

Pierre did not pause. He hammered rivet after rivet, each one a step closer to completion. His arms shook; sweat dripped into his gloves and stung his eyes. The air was thick with dust from the iron and the heat of the metal. He took brief pauses only to catch his breath or wipe his face.

“Pierre,” came the voice of his foreman, Jean‑Baptiste again, “you look tired.”

“I will finish this,” Pierre replied, not looking up. His voice was rough but steady. “We have only a few more hours left before the fair opens.”

Jean‑Baptiste nodded and added, “Your work is important. Keep it going.” He turned back to his own tasks.

On March 29, as dawn approached, Pierre felt something shift in him. The tower seemed less like an obstacle and more like a companion. Its iron ribs, the very ones he had hammered into place, were now part of him. Each rivet he set was a promise—of safety, of progress, of his own future.

He thought of Marie again, her smile from the kitchen window. He imagined their son or daughter growing up in that same apartment, looking out at the tower and knowing they had helped build it.

He took another hammer blow; the rivet clicked into place with a satisfying thud. The metal clinked as it settled. A small sigh escaped him, and he looked down to see his fellow workers staring back at him, their faces reflecting a mixture of relief and pride.

“Pierre,” Jean‑Baptiste said again, “you have done well. We are almost finished.”

The tower was complete by the end of March 30. By that time, the iron structure had been assembled from 18 038 rivets—a testament to the labor of hundreds of men and women working under the guidance of Gustave Eiffel’s company. The final row of rivets on the fourth level had been hammered into place just hours before dawn, securing the tower’s apex.

Jean‑Baptiste had brought a new rivet gun that afternoon—an electric hammering device that could drive rivets faster than a hand mallet. Pierre clamped it onto the frame and let its rhythmic thrum echo through his bones as he hammered the last few rivets. The machine’s hum seemed to merge with the wind, turning the tower’s final completion into a mechanical song.

On the morning of March 31, the day of the World’s Fair opening, Pierre descended to the ground below.

A crowd had gathered at the Champ de Mars. The air smelled of fresh paint and iron. The sound of excited chatter filled the space. Men in top hats, women in long skirts, and families from all over France—and beyond—murmured about the new marvel that would be unveiled that day. The Eiffel Tower was no longer a skeletal structure but a gleaming monument against the sky.

The world seemed to pause for a moment, holding its breath as the tower emerged fully formed from the scaffolding that had once been a maze of iron and rope.

Pierre felt something shift inside him—an affirmation that he had done what his father promised: to build honor into iron. He could hear his father's voice in his mind again, “Your work is not just rivets; it's the future.” And with that thought, he let himself breathe slowly.

The Eiffel Tower was now complete, standing tall over Paris as a testament to human ingenuity. Pierre stood beneath its iron ribs, feeling the weight of his work settle into his chest like a heavy stone. He felt both relief and triumph. He had raced against time, but he had won. The World’s Fair opened that day, and the tower shone bright for the first time.

He turned back to the crowd, letting the laughter and chatter wash over him. It was not only a victory of engineering; it was a victory of heart.

He felt a sense of belonging, as if he had carved his own name into the iron and the history of France.

The tower would stand for centuries to come—a symbol of progress—and Pierre would remember that day forever: when the last rivet was hammered into place and the world watched in awe as the iron spine rose into the sky.

**The Last Rivet**

March 28, 1889

A faint mist curled along the Seine as workers gathered on the Champ de Mars. The morning air was cool and tinged with the scent of freshly cut pine from the scaffolding that spiraled around what would become France’s most daring monument. Below the iron lattice, a thousand rivets had already been hammered into place; above, the tower still stretched toward an indifferent sky, its ribs catching the first blush of dawn.

Pierre Dubois stood on a scaffold, his gloves stained black with the sweat of a hard day. He had come to Paris from Brittany two years earlier, clutching only a promise written in his father’s calloused hand: “If you build the iron, you will earn honor.” The weight of that pledge pressed against his chest like a second set of hands.

The tower itself was a marvel of engineering—a lattice of wrought‑iron and steel, assembled by 300 men and women who toiled under Gustave Eiffel’s watchful eye. By now the structure had taken up more than 7,300 tonnes of iron; its skeleton still held 18 038 rivets, each a small disk about an inch across, waiting to be driven into place.

Pierre was in his element on the third tier, where the beams began to lean toward the sky. The scaffold’s wooden planks creaked under his boots as he moved with practiced ease, aligning the iron plates before hammering the rivet. A sudden gust of wind sent a shiver down the tower; Pierre felt it brush against his face like a cold hand.

He glanced down—no more than thirty meters below—and the world seemed to tilt. The Seine looked like a ribbon of liquid glass, and the city spread out in a maze of rooftops and cobblestones. A vertigo that was not entirely new tugged at him. He had felt it before, when he first climbed above the second tier, when his heart beat so fast he could hear its rhythm against his ribs. For months he kept this fear locked away, hiding it behind a mask of hard work and quiet determination.

His foreman, Jean‑Baptiste, a man with a scar above his left eyebrow from an early accident, stood near the scaffold’s edge, watching the men at their tasks. “Pierre,” he called out, voice echoing across the iron lattice, “you’re working late again. Are you sure you’re fit for this?”

Pierre forced a grin that didn’t quite reach his eyes. “All good, Jean‑Baptiste. Just tired from the day's work.” He didn’t mention the vertigo that made his stomach turn; he could not risk the foreman thinking he was weak.

The tower’s progress had been steady but slow. The first two years of construction were marked by delays caused by rain and the sheer difficulty of working with such a massive structure. Now, as March approached its end, the countdown to the opening of the Exposition Universelle grew longer. There were only three days left until the fair opened on March 31, and Pierre could feel the pressure that pressed against his shoulders.

He moved from one rivet to another, each blow of the hammer a note in a rhythm he had played for months. The iron’s clink echoed through the scaffold like a drumbeat. He remembered how many rivets remained: 1,200 on the fourth tier alone. Each one was a promise—safety, progress, honor.

At the top of the third tier, Pierre paused to rest his hand on the rail. His eyes drifted downward again. The world below seemed to shrink into a point, and he felt the familiar sting of fear that had gnawed at him since he first climbed above the second tier. He took a deep breath, inhaling the cold air that smelled faintly of iron dust.

His heart hammered against his ribs. He could hear it almost louder than the hammer’s clang. The foreman’s voice came from below: “Pierre! Don’t let yourself be distracted. We need every rivet in place before the fair opens.” Jean‑Baptiste had always been supportive, but he had no idea of the battle Pierre fought within his own mind.

Pierre forced himself to focus on the iron plates and the small disk that waited between them. He imagined his father’s voice, steady and sure: “You’ve got this, son. Honor is earned by perseverance.” The memory steadied him enough to set down his hammer and move forward again.

The final row of rivets lay ahead—a long, straight line on a platform that hung above the fourth tier. The height was more than thirty meters from the ground. Pierre had never climbed that high before; the scaffold’s rail ran along the edge of an open space where a rope harness would catch him if he slipped.

As he approached the last rivet, a sudden crack echoed across the iron lattice—his rope had slipped for a fraction of a second. He clung to the harness with both hands as the wind whipped around him. For a heartbeat, his body was suspended in an impossible stillness that felt like time standing still. The fear he had hidden behind his work surged forward: “What if I fall? What if I break my promise?” But he thought of Marie’s face—her eyes wide with anticipation for their unborn child—and the image steadied him again.

He gripped the harness, pulled himself back into place, and let out a sharp breath. The rope caught him, and he felt the familiar tug of safety. He could see the last rivet as a small, dark circle on the plate—a tiny door to the world below. It was now or never.

Pierre lifted his hammer again, heart racing like a drum. Each strike echoed through the tower. The iron clinked against the steel as he drove the rivet into place. He felt a surge of adrenaline; the fear that had once made him tremble seemed to fuse with the determination that kept his hands steady.

One by one, the last rivets were hammered in. The final blow was a thud that resonated through the scaffold like an applause. A moment after the hammer fell, Pierre looked up at the tower’s apex, its iron ribs glinting under the March sun. He could see every corner of Paris from this height—a city that seemed to hold its breath as if waiting for something monumental.

He let out a long, shaky exhale. His foreman appeared behind him, eyes wide with relief and pride. “You did it,” he said, voice thick with emotion. “The tower is finished before the fair opens. You’ve earned your honor.”

Pierre forced a smile that now seemed genuine rather than rehearsed. The fear that had haunted him for months slipped away like the mist that had lifted from the Seine.

He descended the scaffold, each step steady, and walked into his modest apartment on Rue de l'Ancienne Légion. Marie was there, her hand resting on her swollen belly, eyes shining with love and hope. He wrapped an arm around her, feeling the weight of his own fear lift like a stone from his chest.

“Marie,” he whispered, “we’re ready.” She nodded, her smile wide and bright as if she could see the tower’s silhouette in the window behind him.

That evening, after their simple dinner, Pierre stood at the balcony overlooking the Seine. He looked up toward the sky where the Eiffel Tower now gleamed like a silver spine against the city’s horizon. The fear that had once made his stomach turn was replaced by an awe that filled his chest. He could see the world below—the river, the rooftops, the people moving along the cobblestones—without feeling it as a drop.

He thought of his father’s promise again and felt a quiet pride that did not depend on whether he had finished a rivet or not. It was in the act of pushing forward, of confronting the fear that once threatened to hold him back. The tower stood tall; so did Pierre—stronger than he had imagined.

When the fair opened three days later, the Eiffel Tower would shine under the Parisian sky, drawing crowds from all corners of the world. In the heart of the city, a man who had hidden his fear for months watched it all with a quiet satisfaction. The tower’s iron lattice glimmered in the light, a testament not only to engineering but also to the human spirit that had built it, one rivet at a time.

**The Last Night on the Platform**

It was March 30, 1889.  
The sun had slipped below the Seine’s horizon, leaving only a thin ribbon of twilight to hang over the Champ de Mars. The iron lattice of the Eiffel Tower loomed like a skeletal dragon, its unfinished ribs reaching toward a sky that was about to be pierced by dawn.

Pierre Dubois stood on the tower’s upper platform—a narrow, wooden walk stretched between beams that were still half‑assembled. Below him, the city swam in a hazy glow; it was all he could see of Paris from this height. Above, the unfinished tower looked like a ship’s mast awaiting its final sails.

The lanterns they carried cast a flickering amber light over the ironwork. Each beam was a promise that still needed to be sealed with a rivet—a tiny disk that would lock two plates together forever. The last row of those rivets lay in front of Pierre, waiting for his hammer.

“Pierre,” Jean‑Baptiste called from the opposite end of the platform, his voice rough with fatigue but clear over the wind. “We’ve got an hour left. No more delays.” His hand was on a harness strap that would keep him safe if the world fell away below. He slid it over Pierre’s shoulders without looking at him.

Pierre tightened the strap and turned to face the row of plates. The weight of his fear pressed against his ribs; he had hidden it from Jean‑Baptiste for months, telling himself it was just nerves. Tonight, however, the wind felt like a living thing that could snap any moment, and every creak of the iron seemed to echo in his ears.

He lifted the hammer—a heavy wooden mallet—into his hand. The metal plates shivered beneath his fingers as he aligned the first rivet. He hit it once; the sound rang out, reverberating through the scaffold. He followed with a second blow that drove the rivet into place. Each click was a tiny victory against the vertigo that threatened to swallow him.

“Keep going,” Jean‑Baptiste’s voice came again from the far end of the platform. “The fair opens at dawn. We can’t afford a delay.” The foreman’s words were sharp, but Pierre could hear his own heart beating in his ears. He felt the cold metal of the rivet against his palm and the wind whipping past him like a living breath.

A sudden gust rattled the beams. The platform shuddered, and for an instant, Pierre lost his footing. He clutched the rail with both hands, feeling the roughness of iron under his fingers. His harness caught him before he fell; a subtle jolt that reminded him how precarious everything was.

The night pressed on. Lanterns sputtered and glowed, the wind grew louder, and the city below seemed to pulse in the distance. Pierre’s breath came in short bursts as he hammered rivet after rivet. The rhythm of his hammer became a metronome for his fear—each beat a reminder that he was alive, still anchored.

Time slipped by in minutes and then hours. At 11 p.m., Jean‑Baptiste glanced at the clock mounted on a metal bracket near the rail: 12:00 a.m. – “Halfway there.” The foreman’s eyes flicked to Pierre as if measuring his determination. He had been watching him since he’d first joined this shift, and he could see that Pierre was fighting something far larger than the iron.

“Pierre,” Jean‑Baptiste said again, softer now. “You’ve done well. Just one more row.” The words were a lifeline thrown to a man who felt like he might be drowning in his own fear.

The night deepened. The lanterns flickered as the wind grew colder, and Pierre’s breath turned visible in the air. He could feel the weight of the day’s work pressing against him; each rivet was a step toward the promise his father had etched on his palm: “Honor is earned by perseverance.”

At 2 a.m., the first hint of light began to creep over the horizon, painting the tower’s lattice in a faint gold. The city below woke slowly, but Pierre still worked—his hammer striking with steady rhythm.

He reached the final row of rivets that would lock the fifth tier into place. His hands were slick with sweat; his heart pounded so loud he could hear it in the metal around him. He placed the last rivet between two plates and lifted the hammer high, letting gravity do its work. The impact was a bright clang that echoed across the iron skeleton of the tower.

The wind stopped for an instant, as if holding its breath. Then, slowly, dawn broke over Paris. Light poured onto the unfinished platform, bathing it in a warm glow. Pierre stood still for a moment, breathing in the new day and feeling the tension in his chest ease.

Jean‑Baptiste walked to him, a grin spreading across his weathered face. “You did it,” he said. “We’re on schedule. The fair will open at sunrise.”

Pierre lowered his hammer, wiping sweat from his brow. He felt the harness against his shoulders and realized that, for all its coldness, it was a symbol of the safety he had earned by facing his fear.

He looked out over the platform where the iron beams stretched into the sky—a skeleton now complete, a testament to human ingenuity and perseverance. The tower stood ready to welcome the world at sunrise, its iron ribs shining in the first light.

Below, Paris stirred awake, unaware of the night’s quiet triumph that had taken place on a narrow scaffold above them. Pierre felt a sudden surge of pride. He had hidden his fear for months, but now he’d confronted it and won. The tower was finished before the fair opened, and with it, he earned the honor that had been promised to him by his father’s words.

As the first rays of sun kissed the Eiffel Tower’s iron spine, Pierre stepped back from the platform, feeling both humbled and invincible—a riveter who had faced the heights within himself and emerged victorious.

**The Secret Reinforcement**

It had not been a simple act of defiance. It was an act born of years on iron and a mind that never stopped questioning what he saw. Pierre’s foreman, Jean‑Baptiste, had given him direct orders: *“Do not alter any joint or modify the engineer’s plans. The designers have done their calculations.”* Yet one particular joint—where the two main girders met at the fourth tier—had a small but unsettling tremor that did not settle even after several rounds of rivets.

Pierre had spent nights on the platform, alone with his thoughts and the faint hum of wind. He could see the joint’s slight misalignment: the angle was off by a fraction of a degree, enough to create a point of stress he believed would become a failure under the tower’s weight. The engineers’ calculations, he thought, had been too optimistic; they did not account for the cumulative load of each beam and the dynamic forces that wind would impose on an unfinished structure.

He was told by Jean‑Baptiste: *“The plans are final.”* He was told to trust the design. But Pierre had a different instinct—a gut feeling that if this joint failed, the tower could collapse into a storm of iron. He could not let that happen. The risk was too great; the fear of heights had already made him feel powerless. To save the structure and keep his own fear from turning into catastrophe, he had to act.

So, in secret, Pierre had taken a piece of wrought‑iron plate—a hidden spare—stored beneath one of the lanterns that hung on the platform. He slid it into place beneath the joint, aligning it so it would be invisible when the rivets were hammered into the existing plates. The extra plate was a subtle reinforcement: a small wedge that would distribute the load more evenly across the joint.

He had hidden this work in the dead of night, when the wind carried away the sound of his hammer and no one could see him. He used the lantern’s dim light to guide his hands, carefully positioning the plate before securing it with an extra rivet—one that he would not mention when asked about missing components.

The secret was his alone until a moment came when Jean‑Baptiste had to confront a minor irregularity in the joint. The foreman had noticed a subtle misalignment and asked Pierre if he had altered anything. Pierre’s heart pounded, but he answered honestly: *“No, sir.”* He kept quiet about the extra plate.

The night of March 30, when the final rivets were hammered into place, Pierre paused for a moment to look at the joint he had secretly reinforced. The wind whispered through the iron, and his mind recalled the decision that had been made in silence. He remembered how Jean‑Baptiste’s orders clashed with his own judgment, and yet he had chosen safety over obedience.

In the dim glow of lanterns, he felt a surge of relief. He had done what he thought was necessary to keep Paris safe and himself from succumbing to his fear. When dawn broke, the city awoke unaware that on a narrow platform above them a riveter had risked everything to make sure the iron skeleton held.

Pierre’s secret reinforcement became part of the tower’s unspoken story—a quiet testament to the courage of those who work unseen in the shadows of history. It was a small, hidden act of defiance that ensured the great iron lattice would stand for generations, and it gave Pierre a deeper sense of honor than any rivet alone could provide.

Pierre lowered the hammer, wiping sweat from his brow. He felt the harness against his shoulders and realized that, for all its coldness, it was a symbol of the safety he had earned by facing his fear.

He looked out over the platform where the iron beams stretched into the sky—a skeleton now complete, a testament to human ingenuity and perseverance. The tower stood ready to welcome the world at sunrise, its ribs gleaming in the first light.

Below, Paris stirred awake, unaware of the quiet triumph that had taken place on a narrow scaffold above them. Pierre felt a sudden surge of pride. He had hidden his fear for months, but now he’d confronted it and won. The tower was finished before the fair opened, and with it, he earned the honor that had been promised to him by his father’s words.

---

**The Secret Reinforcement**

It had not been a simple act of defiance. It was an act born of years on iron and a mind that never stopped questioning what he saw. Pierre’s foreman, Jean‑Baptiste, had given him direct orders: *“Do not alter any joint or modify the engineer’s plans. The designers have done their calculations.”* Yet one particular joint—where the two main girders met at the fourth tier—had a small but unsettling tremor that did not settle even after several rounds of rivets.

Pierre had spent nights on the platform, alone with his thoughts and the faint hum of wind. He could see the joint’s slight misalignment: the angle was off by a fraction of a degree, enough to create a point of stress he believed would become a failure under the tower’s weight. The engineers’ calculations, he thought, had been too optimistic; they did not account for the cumulative load of each beam and the dynamic forces that wind would impose on an unfinished structure.

He was told by Jean‑Baptiste: *“The plans are final.”* He was told to trust the design. But Pierre had a different instinct—a gut feeling that if this joint failed, the tower could collapse into a storm of iron. The risk was too great; the fear of heights had already made him feel powerless. To save the structure and keep his own fear from turning into catastrophe, he had to act.

So, in secret, Pierre had taken a piece of wrought‑iron plate—a hidden spare—stored beneath one of the lanterns that hung on the platform. He slid it into place beneath the joint, aligning it so it would be invisible when the rivets were hammered into the existing plates. The extra plate was a subtle reinforcement: a small wedge that would distribute the load more evenly across the joint.

He had hidden this work in the dead of night, when the wind carried away the sound of his hammer and no one could see him. He used the lantern’s dim light to guide his hands, carefully positioning the plate before securing it with an extra rivet—one that he would not mention when asked about missing components.

The secret was his alone until a moment came when Jean‑Baptiste had to confront a minor irregularity in the joint. The foreman had noticed a subtle misalignment and asked Pierre if he had altered anything. Pierre’s heart pounded, but he answered honestly: *“No, sir.”* He kept quiet about the extra plate.

The night of March 30, when the final rivets were hammered into place, Pierre paused for a moment to look at the joint he had secretly reinforced. The wind whispered through the iron, and his mind recalled the decision that had been made in silence. He remembered how Jean‑Baptiste’s orders clashed with his own judgment, and yet he had chosen safety over obedience.

In the dim glow of lanterns, he felt a surge of relief. He had done what he thought was necessary to keep Paris safe and himself from succumbing to his fear. When dawn broke, the city awoke unaware that on a narrow platform above them a riveter had risked everything to make sure the iron skeleton held.

---

**The Morning of the Fair**

At first light, as the sun’s pale fingers brushed the tower’s ribs, Jean‑Baptiste and the other workers climbed the final stretch of the platform. The air was cool, still, with only the faint hum of the wind. They moved in hushed steps, checking rivets, tightening bolts, making sure every joint shone like a promise.

Pierre waited at the far end, his hands resting on the railing, watching the light play across the iron. He could feel the weight of what he had done—his secret reinforcement—pressing against his chest like a silent oath.

Jean‑Baptiste reached the fourth tier and stopped in front of the joint that Pierre had altered. His eyes narrowed as he scanned the plates. The rivets looked ordinary, but one was out of place—a small, extra one that did not match the pattern of the others. He frowned, then paused, hand hovering over the unexpected rivet.

“Pierre?” he called, his voice echoing off the iron. “What’s this?”

The riveter turned slowly, eyes wide with the realization that someone had indeed taken a risk beyond what was prescribed. The morning light made the extra rivet glint like a hidden jewel.

Jean‑Baptiste’s gaze flicked to Pierre, who met his stare without flinching. The foreman lifted the hand of the unsuspected rivet and held it up for all to see. He ran a finger over its smooth surface, then turned back to Pierre with an expression that was part disbelief, part respect.

“Your work is… commendable,” Jean‑Baptiste said quietly, “but you should have told me.” The words hung between them like the wind’s whisper across the tower’s ribs. Pierre could feel his heart beating against his ribs once more, but this time it wasn’t fear—it was a steadier pulse of quiet pride.

The foreman nodded, then turned to the rest of the crew and began to explain what he had just seen. The tower would open to the world that day, and all would marvel at its beauty—yet there would be a story hidden in its iron skeleton, written by a riveter who dared to bend the rules for safety.

The morning sun rose higher, illuminating the Eiffel Tower’s gleaming lattice. Jean‑Baptiste stepped forward, placing his hand on Pierre’s shoulder. “Let us finish this together,” he said. “And next time, let us do it as one.”

Pierre nodded, feeling a surge of relief wash over him. He had saved the tower and himself, but now he would share the secret with those who mattered.

The Eiffel Tower opened to the public that day, its iron ribs shimmering in the sun, while the foreman’s discovery of the extra rivets lingered like an unspoken promise—a testament to the quiet bravery of a man who had dared to change the course of history from within.

I keep my hymn book on the stretcher beside me. I am a volunteer nurse working in an overcrowded field hospital during the 1918 influenza pandemic, and I use the worn leather cover as a quiet refuge. Its leather cover feels worn smooth from years of handling, and I keep it close as I write names in the margins. The first patient arrives at 12:03 a.m., lungs heaving with each breath; the smell of fever and disinfectant thick around him. I record his name—Thomas L.—in the margin, a quick cross beside it, the date I note below. There is no formal ledger here; the official one sits in the front office, crisp and cold, a stark reminder of mortality that I cannot bear.

The night is quiet except for the low hum of generators and distant coughs echoing down the corridor. I am alone at my post, but the weight of every life in this cramped hall presses against me. The field hospital is a patchwork of tents, church halls, and commandeered warehouses; beds stack like blocks, linens torn from laundry carts. There are no formalities here; we have to do what we can.

At 2:45 a.m., a young woman named Ruth comes in clutching her chest, breath ragged. She coughs hard, and for a moment I feel a pang of pity; I want to do more than simply write down the name. I offer her a cold cloth and wipe her face with my sleeve. My own throat is raw too, but I keep it quiet. The nurse's uniform feels heavy on my shoulders; I cannot afford to look ill.

The first signs of my own influenza come at 4:10 a.m.: a slight fever rises in the back of my neck, a tickle turns into a cough when I inhale sharply. I force myself to breathe through my nose and keep my hands steady as I bandage a wound on an elderly man's arm. My fingers tremble just enough that I pause for a breath before writing the name—Eleanor B.—in the margin.

The field hospital is running low on supplies; gauze is one of the most scarce items we have. At 7:00 a.m., we run out of gauze; the supply officer takes the last roll and hands it to me with a curt nod. I look at my list in the hymn book and see that there are more patients than there is gauze. The air feels thicker now, the smell of sweat mixing with the antiseptic. I realize we cannot wrap everyone properly.

I take the last roll of gauze and try to stretch it thin, cutting strips as long as I can. In the meantime, I rummage through a stack of newspaper left over from a previous shipment, tearing out thick sheets, folding them into makeshift bandages. The patients stare at me with wide eyes; some weep silently. I cannot keep up with the pace.

At 9:30 a.m., a cough echoes down the corridor that does not belong to any patient. It is my own cough, sharp and unrelenting, but I hide it behind a prayer I whisper into the hymn book. The words are not from memory; they are something I make up on the spot, a plea for strength.

I keep writing names in the margins as the day unfolds. The hospital is crowded, beds packed like sardines. I feel the heat of bodies and the chill of winter wind that seeps through broken windows. My hands ache from handling bandages and writing. The hymn book becomes my lifeline; its pages are a quiet testament to the lives we cannot save.

At 12:45 p.m., the supply officer returns with a fresh roll of gauze, but it is half as long as before. I realize our shortage is critical in the hours ahead. The new roll slides into my hymn book for future use, and I tuck it under a folded newspaper sheet to keep it dry.

I hide my symptoms from everyone, including myself; if I admit feeling ill, someone might ask me to rest or send me home. I cannot afford that; too many people need me.

At 3:00 p.m., the sun is high in the sky and patients' cries are louder than the generator's whine. The temperature inside rises like a furnace. I am on my feet, moving from bed to bed, wrapping arms with gauze strips that feel like paper, writing names as each patient dies or succumbs to exhaustion. The hymn book is almost full; its margins are filled with cramped letters and small crosses.

At 5:30 p.m., the first relief shift arrives in the doorway. They look tired but determined, faces lined by the same strain I feel. They ask me how we are doing, what supplies remain. I answer honestly about gauze and improvised bandages. They hand me a new roll of gauze, which I tuck into my hymn book for future use.

I keep writing names in the margins as evening descends. The night is long; wind whistles through broken shutters. My throat feels raw; each cough is a small betrayal. I cover it with my sleeve and press my hand to my chest, feeling a pulse that races.

At 8:00 p.m., the last patient dies in the third bed from the front. Her name—Miriam S.—is added with an X beside it. The hymn book feels heavy in my hands; its pages feel like a weight on my shoulders. I am exhausted, but I do not stop.

The hours pass slowly, each minute dragging through the night as the hospital hums around me. My own fever rises to 101 °F, skin clammy, breathing shallow. I hide this from everyone, including myself; I am a volunteer, and I cannot bear to be taken out of service.

At 10:00 p.m., I hear the distant clang of a bell as the new shift begins to move through the hall. They bring fresh linens, but we still lack gauze. I feel my body weakening under the weight of the hymn book in my hands. The last page is filled with names; each one is a story that refuses to fade.

At 11:45 p.m., I am at my post again, writing in the margins as an old man coughs his final breath. His name—Samuel P.—is written with a shaky hand. I try to steady myself by clenching my fist around the hymn book. The weight of it presses against my chest, and my heart pounds.

At 12:00 p.m., the new shift arrives in full force; they are ready to take over after my thirty‑six‑hour shift. They ask me how many patients remain. I look at the tally: almost fifty names, all crossed out with an X. My eyes burn as I read them again, each name a memory that refuses to fade.

I am so tired and feverish that my knees buckle. I try to stand, but a wave of exhaustion washes over me. The hymn book slips from my grasp, pages fluttering like wings in the wind. It is then that I collapse at my post—my body unable to bear the weight of the day and the burden of the lives I record.

The relief shift rushes forward; they see me lying on the floor, the hymn book open beside me, its margins crowded with names. They call for help, but it is too late.

**A Fevered Duty**

The night of June 12, 1918, the wind howled through the canvas walls of Camp Hospital No. 3 as if it were trying to carry away every breath that lingered in the air. The tents were a maze of yellow and green cloth stretched over timber frames, their seams patched with rope and old tarpaulins. Inside, the hum of gas lamps was interrupted by the groan of patients coughing into the darkness.

I had arrived at the front two months earlier, clutching my ledger of names and a pack of hand‑made bandages. The American Red Cross had called for volunteers to tend to the wounded, but when I stepped through the gates of this makeshift hospital, it became clear that the real call was for those willing to face a disease that was sweeping across the trenches like a second war.

The first thing I noticed was the sheer number of bodies. A hundred and twenty cots were crowded in a single ward, each occupied by soldiers whose faces had turned pale under their woolen blankets. The air smelled of sweat, antiseptic, and something metallic—blood on the floorboards, perhaps from an earlier casualty that had not yet been cleared.

I was assigned to the influenza ward, a section where the coughs were loud enough to drown out the distant artillery. It was here I met Private James M. Collins, a thirty‑year‑old from Wisconsin, who’d been in the trenches for five months and now lay there with his eyes closed, his breath coming in short, ragged bursts. He had a scar on his left cheek—a souvenir of a stray shell—and he looked up at me as if expecting something miraculous.

“Sir,” he rasped, “I’m not… I’ve been ill for days.”

I handed him a small cup of water and an aspirin tablet. Aspirin was the only thing that could numb the feverish ache, but even it did little to quell the high fever that made his skin feel like it had been wrapped in coal.

“Rest,” I whispered, because there were no other options. The nurses and doctors were stretched thin; we had a supply of morphine for the most severe cases, but by the end of each shift, the stock was dwindling to a handful of vials.

I could not help but feel the weight of that decision. How do you decide who receives what? In a world where a single dose can mean life or death, I felt my own heart beating against my ribs like an enemy soldier in the night.

The following morning, Thomas McLeod—a boy no older than ten—was brought to us from the front lines with a fever of 104°F. He clutched his chest as if it were on fire. His mother had died months ago, and he was the only one left to bring news back home. I knelt beside him and wrapped my hand over his small chest, whispering stories of the stars outside these walls.

“Did you know,” I told him, “that the night sky is full of bright points that have been there since before any man could have imagined?” He nodded solemnly, a tear sliding down his cheek. In the hours that followed, he coughed again and again, and then—suddenly—the world went quiet.

I sat with him until the sun rose, feeling the weight of my own exhaustion pressing against me like a second skin. I did not know how to say goodbye to a boy who had never known what it was to be born in a city that would someday have a name on a map and not a battlefield.

The war outside the tents did not pause for any of us. Sirens wailed, artillery boomed, and the endless march of men and machines continued. Yet inside this makeshift sanctuary, the real enemy was the invisible influenza that had taken the lives of soldiers who had once marched side by side with me in training drills back home.

I wore a mask made of gauze over my nose and mouth—a simple cloth that could not block the virus but offered a small comfort to the patients. I knew that when I walked through the corridor, the air was filled with the scent of feverish breath, and each cough seemed to echo across the floorboards like an accusation.

In the middle of one night, after the last patient had been turned out and the camp fell into a hushed vigil, I heard a muffled cry. The nurse next to me, Marjorie from Maine, was shaking her head as if she could not believe what she saw. She pointed to a cotted bed where a soldier lay motionless.

“I didn’t… I didn’t think—” Marjorie whispered, voice trembling. “He’s gone.”

The man was 28, a young officer who had been wounded in the first days of the war and had since recovered only to be hit by influenza. His chest had stopped moving as suddenly as his breath had started to falter. The world seemed to tilt for a moment, then steady itself.

I sat with Marjorie, and we both cried silently over the loss of another life that was cut short not by bullets but by an unseen enemy. We were both volunteers—women who had come from small towns to help heal the wounded. Our voices were thin, our hearts heavy, and yet we did not stop working.

The influenza epidemic changed how we tended to the soldiers. The wards became more crowded than ever. We learned to triage in ways that felt almost cruel: a patient with a high fever but no severe injuries might be given an aspirin tablet and sent home, while a man with a lung infection received morphine because his breathing was in danger. There were moments when I found myself making a decision in the dim glow of a gas lamp, feeling as if my life was a small part of a larger tragedy.

I had once read about how influenza could cause a “secondary bacterial pneumonia,” and that it was deadly because there were no antibiotics. The doctors spoke in hushed tones about how they could only do so much with what they had: boiled broth for hydration, the best possible bandages, the most efficient use of limited supplies.

I kept a small notebook on my chest—a journal I wrote into when I could find a quiet corner or when the night was still and the wind outside seemed to carry no sound. In it, I recorded the names of those who had passed, their ages, the circumstances, and sometimes a small note about how they were remembered in front of me. “Private James M. Collins—pale, cough; last seen alive at 5:32 a.m.” “Thomas McLeod—smiled for the first time after the first dose of aspirin.”

The war itself was ending when the influenza took its final toll. Soldiers returned home, but many were already sick and dying from a disease that had no cure. The field hospital eventually closed, leaving behind a trail of empty cots and the lingering smell of antiseptic.

On my last night there, as I sat on a wooden bench with my notebook open, I thought about what it meant to volunteer in such a setting. It was not just about tending wounds or giving aspirin; it was about holding onto humanity in the face of an unseen enemy that made even the most ordinary moments feel precious.

I closed my notebook and lifted my head to see the dark sky above. The stars were out, each one a tiny point of light that seemed indifferent to the suffering below. Yet to me, they felt like beacons—a reminder that even in the darkest times, there was still something beyond us that could not be harmed.

When I finally left Camp Hospital No. 3, my hands were trembling with exhaustion and grief. The soldiers who survived had stories to tell about a nurse who stayed late into the night, a woman who carried an army of wounded through their pain and offered a small comfort in her own way. My own story was quiet, written in ink on paper that would soon be folded into a letter home.

I wrote back to my mother:

> “Dear Ma,  
>  I’ve spent the last few weeks at Camp Hospital No. 3. The influenza has taken many of our brothers, but we keep going because it is what we must do. I am tired—tired in more ways than one—but there are moments when a smile from a child or a nod from a soldier gives me hope. I will write again soon if the war allows.  
>  With love,  
>  Ellen”

She answered with a letter that smelled of lavender and the scent of the sea. In it she spoke of how proud she was of her daughter’s courage.

I kept writing in my notebook until there were no more pages left. The ink bled into the paper like the way the influenza had seeped into the lives of everyone around us, leaving a mark that would not be erased.

When I returned home, the world seemed different. The war was over, and yet the memory of the field hospital, of the cramped tents, the coughing soldiers, and the small acts of kindness stayed with me. It taught me that even in the darkest of times, a volunteer nurse’s duty can be both a burden and a blessing—a duty that reminds us that humanity is still present, stubbornly resilient, even when faced with an invisible enemy.

And so I carried on, knowing that each day would bring new challenges, but also new chances to make a difference. The influenza had taught me that the smallest acts of care can be as powerful as any artillery shell. It was not only about tending to wounds but also about tending to hope—an ember that could not be extinguished even by the fiercest storm.

**The Hymnal Ledger**

When Ellen first stepped onto the cracked dirt of Camp Hospital No. 3, she had imagined that her work would be as simple as handing out blankets and tying bandages. The reality was far more brutal: a maze of canvas tents strung over timber frames, a dozen garrisons of patients coughing in unison, and a scent of antiseptic mixed with the metallic tang of blood that seemed to cling to the very walls.

The camp had been built on a former airfield three miles east of the front. By June 1918, it was home to more than two hundred cots, each occupied by a soldier whose face had turned ashen under their woolen blankets. The tents were patched with rope and tarpaulin where the canvas had been torn by the relentless wind that howled through the camp at night.

Ellen had come from a small town in Maine, her mother’s knitting needles in her pocket and a Red Cross uniform on her back. She was young—twenty‑seven—and eager to help. But the first day she saw Private James M. Collins lie on his cot, eyes closed, breathing in short, ragged bursts that sounded like distant artillery shells.

“Sir,” he rasped, “I’ve been ill for days.”

Ellen knelt beside him and offered a cup of water and an aspirin tablet, the only medicine available to ease the fever. She had read the doctor’s orders: morphine for severe cases, aspirin for mild ones. The lack of antibiotics meant that many soldiers would die from complications they could not even comprehend.

After the shift ended, Ellen found herself alone in a corner table where a battered hymnal lay open on its own. The cover was leather, scuffed and cracked; the pages were yellowed with age. She had seen it earlier—a nurse named Mary had slipped it into her own pocket when she left her desk, saying that “the words in these pages have always kept me from losing my mind.” Ellen had taken it for herself without hesitation.

She turned to the margin of a hymn—*Amazing Grace*—and wrote, with a pencil that squeaked on the paper, the name **James M. Collins**. Beneath it she added *June 12*, the date he had died. It was a small act, but in the quiet after the coughs and cries, it felt like something she could hold onto.

The next patient, Thomas McLeod—a boy no older than ten—was brought to her with a fever of 104°F. He clutched his chest as if it were on fire. Ellen wrapped her hand over his small chest, whispering stories of stars outside these walls. When he coughed again and again, she kept a calm face but felt the weight of his death pressing down on her chest.

Later that night, she wrote *Thomas McLeod* beneath *It Is Well With My Soul*, the hymn that had soothed her own nerves in times of hardship. She didn’t keep an official ledger for those names; the Red Cross required a formal logbook where each patient’s details were recorded by number and date. Ellen could not bear to see the sterile page filled with rows of data, each one a cold reminder of loss.

The hymn book became her private tally. Every night, after the last patient had been turned out or died, she would pull it from its corner and write the name of anyone who had passed that day in the margin of a hymn that resonated with his memory. She didn’t mark a date for every entry—sometimes she simply wrote the name, sometimes she added a tiny cross or a heart, sometimes she left it blank, letting the silence between lines hold the grief.

Her hands would tremble when writing *John O’Neill* under *Nearer My God to Thee*. He had been a young officer who had never seen a battlefield before he was sent to this camp. His cough had turned into wheezing, and then—there was no time for mourning—a sudden collapse that left him still as she wrote his name.

The official ledger sat in its drawer, untouched most days. It was the kind of book that held names, dates, admissions, discharges, and a column for “deceased.” Ellen would glance at it once, see the neat rows of ink, and feel her stomach tighten. She imagined each line as an abstraction of a life—no more than numbers and letters to the outside world.

The influenza outbreak was relentless. By July, the number of patients had doubled. The hospital’s capacity seemed to shrink beneath the weight of feverish bodies. Ellen worked 12‑hour shifts with no respite, administering morphine to those whose lungs were failing, offering comfort to those who had lost the will to breathe. Each day she felt her own body wear thin as if it too was a patient.

When a wave of deaths came in early August—twelve patients within 48 hours—Ellen’s fingers shook so hard that the pencil slipped from her hand and landed at the foot of *Abide With Me* with a faint, ragged line. She pressed the paper to her palm and let the tears fall onto the hymnal's pages.

“Why do you keep these names?” Mary asked one afternoon as they shared a brief lunch under a canvas awning that smelled of boiled broth and fear.

Ellen looked up from the hymn book, eyes red but steady. “Because the ledger makes them disappear,” she said. “It’s efficient, it’s cold. In this room, every name is a story. I need to remember each one.”

Mary nodded slowly, as if hearing the truth of it for the first time. She reached into her pocket and pulled out an envelope stamped with the Red Cross seal. Inside were forms—patient admissions, discharge summaries, death certificates. Ellen closed the hymnal gently, set it aside on the table, and took a breath.

She began to fill out the official form as she had always done: name, rank, unit, date of admission, condition, medication administered, and if applicable, the date of death. But when her hand reached for the final line—“deceased”—she paused. The ink felt heavy in her palm. She put the pen down, opened the hymnal again, and wrote *Ellen’s own name* at the bottom of the margin, beneath a simple line that read “for those who cannot be counted.” It was an act of defiance, a private reminder that she would not let these lives become mere entries in a ledger.

The days stretched on. The influenza took its toll—half the patients died within weeks of admission, many from secondary bacterial pneumonia. Ellen’s own health began to falter: her fingers trembled when she wrote names; her chest felt tight each time she thought of a patient who had died while she was away from his cot.

One night, as the wind rattled the canvas walls and a distant artillery shell thundered through the night, Ellen found herself staring at *It Is Well With My Soul* in the hymnal. She began to read the words aloud to the empty room: “When I am in the valley of the shadow of death.” Her voice cracked as she sang along, her own sorrow mixing with the hymn’s comforting cadence.

She felt a hand on her shoulder—a nurse named Margaret, who had been working at the front for months. They shared a moment of silence, each feeling the weight of loss that lay heavy in their hearts. When they finally spoke, Margaret whispered, “You keep writing names, don’t you? It’s… it’s more humane.”

Ellen nodded. “I can’t bear to see them all as numbers,” she said. “They’re not just patients; they’re people. I want to remember them.”

Margaret smiled faintly and pulled a small notebook from her bag. Inside were notes of patients’ last words, the way their eyes crinkled when they laughed, the way a cough would break into a cry. She handed it to Ellen, saying, “If you ever need a place that’s not a hymn book or a ledger, I have this.”

Ellen looked at the notebook, then back at her hymnal. It was as if each of them had found their own method of coping—a private way to honor those who slipped away.

The influenza finally subsided in early September. The camp slowly emptied; patients were transferred to larger hospitals or sent home with a limp and a scar. Ellen stayed for the last weeks, helping to wrap up the hospital’s records, cleaning linens, and comforting the few who remained. She had written more names into her hymnal than she could count—hundreds of entries that now sat in its margins like a secret garden.

When the last patient was discharged, the camp’s tents were taken down, and the land returned to fields, Ellen packed her belongings. In her small bag, along with a needle set and a bundle of bandages, she tucked the hymnal. It had become more than a book; it was a repository of memories that would never be erased.

On her way back to Maine, she stopped at a small village where a church stood on a hill. The bell rang each hour as if calling her home. She walked into the church and found an empty pew. Ellen sat down and opened the hymnal, placing it on her lap. She whispered each name out loud, one by one: *James M. Collins*, *Thomas McLeod*, *John O’Neill*, *Ellen’s own name*. The words floated in the quiet space, mingling with the soft hum of a choir that had begun to sing.

She closed the hymnal gently and set it on her chest, feeling its weight as a comfort against her heart. She turned away from the church and walked down the path back into the world, carrying with her the private ledger that would forever be etched in the margins of a hymn book: a testament that even when official records fail to capture humanity, one can still honor lives by writing their names under the songs that keep them alive.

In the years that followed, Ellen would sometimes find herself turning the pages of that hymnal and seeing the names she had written in faded ink. Each name was a story she carried with her—a reminder that in a time when an invisible enemy swept across trenches and tents, one woman chose to remember each life not as a statistic but as a hymn sung quietly on a cold night under canvas walls.

It was 11:59 p.m., and I found myself standing at the threshold of Camp Hospital No. 3, a place that had become my world for the past two months. The night air was cold and damp; the canvas walls creaked as if they too were tired from holding so many bodies. A faint hiss of gas lamps floated over the corridor, the only light that could keep the darkness at bay.

I pulled the hymn book I carried from my bag, its leather cover cracked by years of use. Inside, a few hymns had already been turned to, each page a quiet testimony to the lives that would soon be added. The margins were thick enough for me to write in—an old habit that had grown into a secret ledger when no one else cared to remember.

The clerk had just left with the last of the day's supplies. I slipped past him and opened the supply closet, my fingers brushing against cold metal. Inside, a small tin of gauze lay on top of a stack of rolled bandages. The tin was almost empty; only three strips remained, each one barely long enough to cover an arm.

I stared at them for a moment—three little pieces of cloth that could mean life or death—and then I turned the tin over and counted: one, two, three. The numbers seemed absurdly small for a field hospital that was already full to its brim with patients who coughed in unison like artillery shells.

The shift began at midnight. I had been assigned to the influenza ward, where coughing soldiers lay on cots that had never seen more than five people each. There were only enough blankets for those who could stand a little, and I knew that as soon as dawn broke, fresh bodies would arrive from the front lines—bodies with fever so high they looked like they had been kissed by the sun.

The first patient of the night was Private James M. Collins. He had been in the trenches for five months, his cheeks gaunt, eyes bright with a stubborn hope that he could still get home. But now he lay on his cot, coughing violently and clutching his left arm where a splinter had wound through muscle. The wound bled thinly; a small gauze pad was all that would be needed if I had any.

I knelt beside him and opened the tin. A single strip of gauze stared back at me—too little to cover a full arm. My hand trembled as I cut it into two pieces, each half a strip long. James lifted his head, eyes closed, then opened them again, a faint smile curling over his lips.

“Sir,” he rasped, “I’m… I’ve been ill for days.”

I handed him a cup of water and an aspirin tablet. The aspirin did little against the fever that had taken hold of him, but it was all we could give. I took the half strip of gauze, pressed it against his wound, then covered it with a clean piece of linen from the supply closet. It wasn’t perfect—there were seams and folds—but it was something.

I tucked the hymn book beside me, opened to *Nearer My God to Thee*, and in the margin I wrote: **James M. Collins**. I added a tiny cross, as if that might be enough to honor him. When he finally slipped into a quiet sleep at 3 a.m., the coughs faded, but my mind was still awake.

By 4 a.m., a new wave of soldiers had arrived from the front. Their faces were gaunt, their breath coming in short, desperate bursts that sounded like dying birds. Among them was Lieutenant Barlow, his uniform torn and a wound on his right thigh where shrapnel had left a jagged scar.

Barlow’s wound bled profusely; the nurse who came to him tried to apply a bandage but found no gauze. He looked at me with eyes that held both fear and gratitude.

“I can’t… I don’t have enough,” he whispered, his voice thin.

I remembered the three strips of gauze left in the tin. The thought of giving them all to one man made my chest tighten. But I had to think of the others—James, the young boy Thomas McLeod who’d been brought in with a fever of 104°F and a cough that sounded like thunder.

The clerk had told me once that we would run out of gauze by morning. The night was short; the day was long.

I tried to decide how best to use what I had. We had some clean cloth from the linens, but it was rough and unwashed. I could cut a piece for Barlow’s wound, then use the rest as a dressing for Thomas’s arm when he came in with a splinter on his left hand—a small wound that required minimal coverage.

The decision felt like choosing which child to give medicine first; it was cruel. The world outside the tents did not care about my choices—it only knew of artillery and of coughing soldiers.

I went back to Barlow, placed a rough piece of cloth over his wound, wrapped it with some linen, and whispered a prayer: *Amazing Grace*. He nodded weakly, then fell into a cough that seemed to shudder through the entire ward. The other patients around us did not notice the change in my hands; they were busy with their own breath.

I pulled out the hymn book again, opened to *Amazing Grace*, and wrote **Lieutenant Barlow** beneath it. I added a small heart next to his name, as if that could keep him from becoming another forgotten number on a ledger. The formal ledger—an oak drawer in the corner with rows of names, dates, and numbers—was too cold for me. It did not honor a dying man; it only counted.

At 6 a.m., the first wave of patients had been treated as best we could. I was exhausted to the point where my fingers shook even when I held the hymn book. My mind kept replaying the names I had written: James, Barlow… and then Thomas McLeod, who would die later that night after a fever that turned his chest into a furnace.

The official nurse, Mrs. McCormick, had come in at 6:30 a.m., her hair disheveled from the night's work. She looked at me with a tired smile and said, “We’re running out of gauze, Ellen. We have to ration.”

I nodded without words. The truth was that we were already rationing—my mind had been making choices for weeks now.

She lifted the small tin again. Inside, there were no more strips. I could see the last piece of cloth on the floor, torn from a blanket used for someone else. It smelled faintly of sweat and antiseptic. The idea of using it as a dressing made my stomach turn.

We had to decide who would receive the final strip of gauze. James M. Collins had died at 1 a.m., but he was gone; I could use his name in the hymn book again for that moment. Thomas McLeod, however, still lay on his cot, coughing like a dying child.

“Give it to him,” I whispered, holding out my hand.

Mrs. McCormick shook her head slowly. “We have to think of everyone.” She looked at me with an expression that said, “I’m not the one to decide who lives or dies.”

The night was a blur. The coughs became louder as more patients fell into fever. The air grew thick and hot; the gas lamps flickered like dying stars.

At 10 p.m., Thomas McLeod’s chest convulsed with an agony that shook the whole ward. I could see the tremor in his ribs, the way his breath came out in sharp, ragged bursts. He had no gauze to cover his wound, and I couldn’t find any clean cloth.

I thought of my hymn book again; it was open to *It Is Well With My Soul*. I pressed a small piece of rough linen over Thomas’s splinter, wrapped it with a bandage I made from the torn blanket. The fabric was not clean, but it was something. As he fell into a deep cough that seemed to shake his whole body, I whispered a prayer.

I wrote **Thomas McLeod** beneath *It Is Well With My Soul*, adding a small line beside his name: “—told me his mother had died in the war.” The words were my own; they were not on the formal ledger. The clerk would later write an entry, but I could not bear to let that cold sheet of paper hold the weight of his life.

The 36 hours passed like a dream and a nightmare rolled into one. By the time the sun rose at 6 a.m., the shift was over; my body shook with exhaustion, and my hands were still shaking when I closed the hymn book.

I sat on the edge of a cot, feeling the roughness of the canvas against my cheek. The night’s events replayed in my mind like an endless loop: the smell of antiseptic, the coughs, the decision to use the last strip of gauze for Thomas McLeod, the names written in hymn margins.

I could feel the weight of each name as I looked at them—James M. Collins, Lieutenant Barlow, Thomas McLeod. The formal ledger sat on its oak drawer with rows of names that would be recorded by someone else; it was a sterile account. Here, in this small book, I had written their lives and deaths in a way that felt personal.

I lifted the hymn book, closed it gently, and placed it back into my bag. The paper smelled faintly of ink and hope. As I walked through the corridor toward the exit, the wind carried with it a faint scent of fresh earth after rain. The night was over; dawn broke across the horizon like a promise that even in the darkest times there would be a light.

I stepped into the morning air, my heart heavy but still beating. I had survived the 36‑hour shift, and in my hymn book, I carried their names forever. It was not enough to save them, but it was all that could honor what we had lost.

Inside, *Amazing Grace* has already been turned twice; the margins are waiting for names that no one else will remember.
